query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys is predominantly governed by kinetically limited surface diffusion rather than solely by the bulk high configurational entropy.
generation.material_initial_state: Well-dispersed, homogeneous high-entropy nanoalloy particles in a single-phase solid solution with no initial phase segregation.
generation.intervention: Perform in situ high-resolution TEM heating experiments comparing nanoalloy particles with a controlled surface passivation coating (to inhibit surface diffusion) versus unpassivated particles.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature conditions (e.g., above 800 °C) in an inert or controlled atmosphere to avoid extrinsic oxidation effects, during which surface and grain boundary diffusion processes are activated.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface atomic mobility and associated interface-driven diffusion processes that lead to phase segregation or chemical ordering.
generation.mechanism: In unpassivated particles, high temperatures promote enhanced surface diffusion that weakens the kinetic barriers at interfaces, leading to early phase segregation and chemical inhomogeneities. In contrast, passivation increases surface energy barriers, suppressing surface diffusion and maintaining the bulk solid solution, thereby stabilizing the structure despite elevated thermal activation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline unpassivated particles, passivated nanoalloy particles will show reduced signs of phase segregation or chemical instability (i.e., more uniform elemental distribution and preserved phase structure) over equal heating durations, as observed by in situ TEM.
generation.baseline: Nanoalloy particles without surface passivation undergoing the same high-temperature treatment.
generation.boundary: This prediction applies to nanoalloys under high-temperature regimes where thermal energy is sufficient to activate surface and grain boundary diffusion (typically >800 °C) and may not extend to conditions where oxidation or extrinsic environmental factors dominate the stability behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of surface diffusion versus bulk configurational entropy is not fully determined; thus, while the trend (passivation leading to enhanced stability) is expected, the precise temperature threshold and exact magnitude of the suppression effect remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy particles: one with a thin, inert surface passivation layer (e.g., an oxide or nitride coating known to restrict surface atom mobility) and one unpassivated. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature conditions (e.g., 800–1000 °C) inside an in situ high-resolution TEM. Monitor and record the evolution of the microstructure and elemental distribution over time.
measurements: High-resolution TEM imaging to observe changes in grain boundary structure and diffusion-related phenomena
EDS mapping during heating to track elemental segregation
Measurement of diffusion rates or onset time for phase segregation in each sample
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated nanoalloy particles exhibit a similar degree of phase segregation and chemical instability (e.g., comparable diffusion rates and loss of homogeneity) as the unpassivated particles under identical high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that surface diffusion is the dominant kinetic factor governing stability would be refuted.

First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys has largely focused on bulk or polycrystalline systems and later on nanocrystalline thin films, where high‐temperature performance was evaluated mostly in terms of overall mechanical, oxidation, or wear behavior. Initial studies relied on processing routes (e.g., sputtering or spark plasma sintering) that produced nano-scale features, but the mechanistic origin of stability was often attributed to broad factors such as configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion. In more recent work, in situ high-temperature characterization (e.g. HTXRD in PMC10384371) has revealed that at elevated temperatures, not only bulk thermodynamics but also nanoscale surface energies and accelerated grain boundary diffusion play key roles in driving chemical segregation, oxidation, or even phase transformations. Thus, the trend moved from attributing stability solely to high configurational entropy toward an acknowledgment that interface- and surface-driven kinetic processes (which are pronounced in nanoalloys) are equally critical.
decision.unsolved: What remains unsolved is the direct identification and quantification of the dominant intrinsic factor governing stability in nanoalloys at high temperatures – specifically, distinguishing whether the thermodynamic stabilization (via high configurational entropy) or the kinetic limitations (e.g., high diffusion barriers at interfaces and surfaces) is primarily responsible. The interplay between interatomic/interfacial energies and enhanced surface diffusion in the nanoscale regime is still ambiguous, and existing work has not isolated these effects with a controlled, comparative experiment.
decision.lever: Performing in situ high-resolution TEM heating experiments on high-entropy nanoalloy particles with and without controlled surface passivation.
decision.why: This approach directly leverages the trend toward nanoscale and dynamic studies at high temperature. By comparing passivated (minimizing surface diffusion and lower surface energy contributions) versus unpassivated particles under the same thermal conditions, one can independently assess the role of surface‐mediated atomic rearrangements versus bulk configurational entropy in governing structural and chemical stability. This controlled comparison specifically addresses the unanswered question by isolating the kinetic (i.e., diffusion/surface effects) contribution against the background of intrinsic high entropy.
